chapters.title: Chapter 3: Completing and Stress-Testing the DCF

lessons.title: Terminal Value: Perpetual Growth vs Exit Multiple

children.text: A five-year DCF forecast feels like the hard work. It is not where most of the value lives. For a typical Indian company, the cash flows you painstakingly forecast for years 1 to 5 account for a minority of the value. The rest comes from a single number representing everything after year 5: the terminal value. Get it wrong and nothing else in the model matters.

body.text: Terminal value is not a plug to make the model finish. It is a claim about what the business looks like when it has stopped growing fast: its growth, its returns on new capital and its risk. The perpetual growth and exit multiple methods must tell the same story. When they do not, one of your assumptions is wrong.

children.text: Why Terminal Value Dominates
You cannot forecast year by year forever, so a DCF has two parts: an explicit forecast period, and a
terminal value
that captures all cash flows beyond it.

markDefs.definition: The value, at the end of the explicit forecast period, of all cash flows from that point onward. It is discounted back to today and added to the present value of the explicit forecast.

body.caption: The terminal value sits at the end of year n and is discounted n years, not n + 1

children.text: Take the disciplined five-year forecast for Kaveri Ridge Cement from the last lesson and discount it at the 11.5% WACC we built in Chapter 2.

body.caption: Kaveri Ridge Cement: present value of the explicit forecast (₹ crore, illustrative)

children.text: Five years of cash flow are worth ₹1,461 crore today. Hold on to that number.
Method 1: Perpetual Growth
The perpetual growth method, also called the Gordon growth method, assumes that after year n the business grows its cash flow at a constant rate forever.

body.caption: Next year's cash flow divided by the gap between the discount rate and perpetual growth

children.text: Rule 1: Growth must be modest

The perpetual growth rate is a forever rate. No company can grow faster than the economy forever, or it would eventually become the economy. For rupee cash flows, keep g at or below long-run nominal GDP growth, and most practitioners go further, capping it near the risk-free rate. With a 10-year G-sec yield around 6.5%, a perpetual growth rate of 4% to 6% is a sensible range for most Indian companies. The formula also breaks completely if g approaches WACC.
Rule 2: Growth must be paid for

This is the rule most models break. Year 6 cash flow is not simply year 5 cash flow plus growth, because a business growing at 5% forever must keep reinvesting to do it. Use the link from Chapter 1: reinvestment rate = g ÷
RONIC

markDefs.definition: Return on new invested capital: the after-tax return a company earns on the capital it reinvests in the future. In a terminal value, it is usually set close to or slightly above WACC, as competition erodes excess returns.

body.caption: Steady-state cash flow after the reinvestment needed to sustain growth g

children.text: For Kaveri Ridge, assume 5.0% perpetual growth and a RONIC of 13.0%, a little above WACC, reflecting a well-run business in a competitive industry.
Discount it back five years: ₹11,363 ÷ 1.7234 = ₹6,594 crore. Now the full picture.

body.title: Kaveri Ridge enterprise value of ₹8,054 crore: where it comes from

body.caption: From enterprise value to value per share (₹ crore unless stated)

body.text: The terminal value is 82% of Kaveri Ridge's enterprise value. That is normal: for most Indian listed companies it sits somewhere between 60% and 85%, and higher still for fast growers. It is why the next lesson's move from enterprise value to value per share, and the lesson after that on sensitivity tables, matter so much.

children.text: Three Terminal Value Mistakes, Quantified

body.caption: Same Kaveri Ridge forecast, three common errors (₹ crore)

cells: Correct: growth with consistent reinvestment, discounted 5 years
Growing year 5 FCFF, which still carries high-growth reinvestment
Correct TV, but discounted 6 years instead of 5

children.text: The first error is by far the most common and the most dangerous. It quietly assumes a company can grow forever without spending a rupee, and it inflates value by a large margin. The second error goes the other way here, because year 5 still carries the reinvestment needed for 7% growth. Both come from skipping Rule 2.
Method 2: Exit Multiple

The exit multiple method assumes the business is sold at the end of year n at a multiple of that year's earnings, most often EV/EBITDA. Investment bankers and many Indian brokerages favour it because it is quick and familiar.

body.caption: Terminal value from a multiple of final-year EBITDA

children.text: Kaveri Ridge's year 5 EBITDA, adding back depreciation at its historical 4.6% of revenue, is ₹1,981 crore. An analyst applies a 9× EV/EBITDA exit multiple, a mid-cycle figure for a mid-sized cement company.

body.title: Kaveri Ridge: the two methods side by side

columns.label: Perpetual growth (5%, RONIC 13%)
points: Terminal value: ₹11,363 crore
Enterprise value: ₹8,054 crore
Value per share: ₹262
Implied exit multiple: 5.7× EBITDA

columns.label: Exit multiple (9× EBITDA)
points: Terminal value: ₹17,832 crore
Enterprise value: ₹11,808 crore
Value per share: ₹412
Implied perpetual growth: 9.7% (at RONIC 13%)

children.text: The two methods disagree by about ₹150 per share. Converting each into the other's language tells you why. A perpetuity at 5.0% growth is equivalent to selling at only 5.7× EBITDA. A 9× exit multiple is equivalent to assuming 9.7% growth forever, above the 6.5% risk-free rate we are using and a high rate for a cement company forever. The exit multiple has quietly imported a far more optimistic long-run story.

body.text: An exit multiple taken from today's trading prices brings today's market mood into your DCF. If cement stocks currently trade at rich multiples, your "intrinsic" value inherits that richness, and the DCF is no longer independent of the market. Always convert an exit multiple into its implied perpetual growth rate, and a perpetual growth assumption into its implied exit multiple. If either looks unreasonable, fix it.

children.text: How Sensitive Is Terminal Value to Growth?
Hold WACC at 11.5% and RONIC at 13.0%, and vary only the perpetual growth rate. Then repeat with RONIC equal to WACC.

body.title: Kaveri Ridge terminal value at year 5 by perpetual growth rate (₹ crore)

children.text: With RONIC at 13%, moving growth from 3% to 7% raises terminal value from ₹10,655 crore to ₹12,545 crore. With RONIC equal to WACC, the line barely moves: it only drifts up because year 6 NOPAT itself is assumed to be higher. That is Chapter 1's lesson again. Growth earned at a return equal to the cost of capital adds almost nothing, so the growth rate only matters if you believe the company keeps earning above its WACC forever.

columns.label: Perpetual growth
points: Grounded in the company's own cash flows and returns
Forces you to state growth, RONIC and WACC explicitly
Very sensitive to g when RONIC is well above WACC
Best as the primary method in an intrinsic valuation

columns.label: Exit multiple
points: Quick, familiar and easy to explain
Imports current market pricing into the DCF
Dangerous when applied to peak-cycle EBITDA
Best as a cross-check, converted into implied growth

body.label: Before accepting any terminal value
body.context: g at or below the risk-free rate and nominal GDP growth; reinvestment consistent with g and RONIC; the terminal year is a normal year, not a peak or a trough; and the implied exit multiple and implied growth rate both look reasonable.

children.text: One more practical point: the explicit forecast must run long enough for the business to reach a steady state before the terminal value begins. Five years is fine for a mature cement company. A fast-growing consumer or technology company may need ten years or more, with growth fading year by year, before a perpetual growth rate makes sense.
Check Your Understanding

body.title: Calculate a terminal value
body.prompt: A company's FCFF in year 6 is expected to be ₹200 crore. Its WACC is 12% and its perpetual growth rate is 5%. What is its terminal value at the end of year 5, in ₹ crore? Round to the nearest crore.
body.explanation: TV = ₹200 ÷ (0.12 - 0.05) = ₹200 ÷ 0.07 = ₹2,857 crore. This is the value at the end of year 5, not today.

body.title: Discount the terminal value
body.prompt: A DCF has a terminal value of ₹10,000 crore at the end of year 5. The WACC is 12%. What is the terminal value worth today, in ₹ crore? Round to the nearest crore.
body.explanation: PV = ₹10,000 ÷ (1.12)⁵ = ₹10,000 ÷ 1.7623 = ₹5,674 crore. Discount over 5 years, the year the terminal value is measured at.

body.title: Choosing a perpetual growth rate
body.question: You are valuing a large Indian FMCG company in rupees. The 10-year G-sec yield is 6.5%. Which perpetual growth rate is most defensible for its terminal value?
options: 12%, because the company has grown at 12% for the last decade
5% to 6%, at or below the risk-free rate and long-run nominal GDP growth
9%, because Indian consumption will keep growing faster than GDP
body.explanation: Perpetual growth is a forever rate, so it should not exceed long-run nominal GDP growth and is usually kept near or below the risk-free rate. Past decade growth belongs in the explicit forecast, fading over time. Zero growth is overly conservative for a rupee-denominated business in a growing, inflationary economy.

body.title: Paying for perpetual growth
body.textWithBlank: In a steady-state terminal value, the reinvestment rate equals the perpetual growth rate divided by the return on ___ invested capital.
body.explanation: Reinvestment rate = g ÷ RONIC. At 5% growth and a 13% RONIC, the company must reinvest 38.5% of NOPAT every year to keep growing.

body.title: The broker DCF with a 25× exit
body.scenario: Farhan, a Kolkata-based investor, reads a brokerage report on a listed specialty chemicals company with a DCF target price 40% above the current market price. The appendix shows: a five-year explicit forecast in which revenue grows 22% a year; a terminal value calculated at 25× year 5 EV/EBITDA, "in line with where the stock trades today"; year 5 EBITDA margin of 28%, compared with a ten-year average of 19%; and terminal value making up 88% of enterprise value. The WACC used is 11%.
body.prompt: What questions should Farhan ask about this terminal value before trusting the target price?
body.modelAnswer:
1. What growth does 25× imply? Converting the exit multiple into a perpetual growth rate, at any sensible RONIC, will likely give a rate close to or above WACC. That means the report is assuming near-permanent high growth, not a steady state.
2. Why use today's trading multiple? Using the stock's current multiple as the exit multiple makes the "intrinsic" value depend on the market price the report is trying to judge. It is partly circular.
3. Is year 5 a normal year? A 28% EBITDA margin against a 19% ten-year average suggests the terminal value is being applied to peak profitability. Specialty chemicals margins are cyclical and competitive.
4. Is five years long enough? A company still growing 22% in year 5 has not reached a steady state. The explicit period should be longer, with growth fading, before a terminal value is applied.
5. How much of the target rests on the terminal value? At 88% of enterprise value, the target price is essentially a bet on the exit multiple and the peak margin. Farhan should re-run the terminal value with a perpetual growth rate of 5% to 6%, a margin near the long-term average and a RONIC modestly above WACC, and see whether the 40% upside survives.

points: Terminal value usually makes up 60% to 85% of a DCF's enterprise value, so it deserves more scrutiny than any single forecast year.
Perpetual growth method: TV = FCFF next year ÷ (WACC - g). Keep g at or below the risk-free rate and long-run nominal GDP growth.
Growth must be paid for: in steady state, reinvestment rate = g ÷ RONIC. Growth without reinvestment inflates value dramatically.
Exit multiple method: TV = exit multiple × final-year EBITDA. It is quick, but imports current market pricing into your DCF.
Always convert each method into the other: the implied exit multiple and the implied perpetual growth rate must both look sensible.
Discount terminal value over n years, apply it only once the business has reached a steady state, and never to a peak or trough year.
